bet.text: Keep everything as simple as possible, after a tendency to over complicate things in the past.

demand.text: In an off-season interview: consistency was super important for the shooter. The team first wanted the fender shot for the consistency of driving up, but prototyping showed it could shoot accurately from farther away, and it chose to be more ambitious. It likes to shoot from the tape of the tarmac to just past the launch pad.

cycle.text: In an off-season interview: green wheels grab cargo and a second set brings it to the middle. Two automated indexer sections each stop when their sensor trips; with both tripped the intake goes up. The team likes to shoot from the tape of the tarmac to just past the launch pad.

endgame.text: In an off-season interview: an arm telescopes up, grabs mid and pulls down; on the way down the bar hits spring hooks that lock on, and the robot climbs to the next level, with pneumatic cylinders moving the arm. The climb is entirely manual and takes about seven seconds to traversal from inside the hangar.

fallback.text: In an off-season interview: because the climb is manual, the operator can adjust on the fly when something goes wrong, without an emergency stop.

gave_up.text: In an off-season interview: the climber takes up a lot of space in the middle of the robot, so the indexer is L-shaped. Neither the shooter's angle nor its relative flywheel speeds adjust; from farther back shots still hit, but the balls go really high.

changed.text: From an off-season interview, undated. Intake: balls got stuck rolling in place until a center wheel of about 4 inches was added. Shooter: a fifth or sixth version; the team kept adding flywheels and it got more consistent. Climber: one cylinder could not keep the bar steady and caused a lot of swing, so a second was added.

outcome.text: 50-18-0 in official play; finalist in the Newton division; ranked 12 of the pooled top 20 (OPR 58.30, Newton).

facts.text: Championship pit data a commenter posted lists a tank drive and no turret
A commenter in March listed it among high quality Pacific Northwest WCD/KOP robots, in a district mostly on swerve
During the division playoffs a commenter said it proved swerve is not needed to be good

solves.text: Center the balls and really contain them, which past indexers had not done

facts.text: In an off-season interview: green wheels in front suck the balls in; a second set brings them toward the middle
Mecanum wheels already in the lab from FTC robots center the balls
A bigger green wheel in the center, about
In an off-season interview: a little padding helps bring the ball in
It goes up by itself when both indexer sensors are tripped

solves.text: Fit around the climber, and spare the operator the many buttons of past years

facts.text: In an off-season interview: a vertical belt and a horizontal belt, so each of two balls has its own section
Photoelectric sensors: each belt stops when its sensor trips
Each stage is a relatively tight timing belt with compliant wheels
The intake rises when both sensors are tripped (another member says when the bottom one is), so the robot pretty much never holds three balls

solves.text: Shoot consistently, and stop what would be a really big bounce-out problem

cost.text: From farther back the shot still hits, but the balls go really high

facts.text: In an off-season interview: about six inches of flywheel, with inertia flywheels; adding flywheels made it more and more consistent
A black flywheel against bounce-outs, at a distance that was tuned a lot
Neither the relative flywheel speeds nor the angle is adjustable
In an off-season interview: iterated on the team's laser cutter, to a fifth or sixth version
